title: Natural selection can modify organisms at any age

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Natural selection can modify organisms at any age

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because variations arising at a particular life stage tend to be inherited at the same stage, natural selection can modify organisms at any age, for instance adapting larvae independently of adults.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: natural selection will be enabled to act on and modify organic beings at any age, by the accumulation of profitable variations at that age, and by their inheritance at a corresponding age.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes”. Scope: all organisms, especially those with distinct life stages such as insects with larvae

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction maps to established stage-structured quantitative-genetic analyses. Existing data demonstrate the process in subsets, but do not span all ages and organismal groups.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate stage-specific heritability and selection gradients for larval, juvenile and adult traits, and test genetic responses at the same life stage. Evidence of heritable fitness variation and evolutionary response at multiple stages supports the mechanism; absence of stage-specific heritability or antagonistic carryover would limit it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Stage-specific inheritance is rarely measured together with lifetime fitness.

Selection at one stage can be confounded by genetic correlations with other stages.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The measurable core is whether characters of different life stages can evolve separately, which quantitative genetics and comparative data can test. Those data are rich for Drosophila and a few other models and thin everywhere else, so the universal and the insect-larva readings are both subset tests. Cross-stage genetic correlation is a real discriminator, but assembling it beyond model organisms would take specialist compilation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate genetic correlations between traits expressed at different ages, and compare phylogenetic divergence of larval and adult characters. Independent, stage-specific responses would confirm that selection can modify one age without the other; consistently high cross-age correlations would refute that independence. Age-specific inheritance is proxied by stage-specific expression and quantitative-genetic matrices.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Pleiotropy across metamorphosis can hide independent modification.

Stage-specific gene expression is not the same variable as age-specific inheritance of a selected trait.

Age-specific genetic-covariance matrices exist for a handful of laboratory species.
